opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and they compound on each other.

The first is just expertise. Historically, to use these tools you needed people who were trained in logic, in theorem proving, in model checking, and there aren't that many of those people in the world. Many of them have PhDs, and they're scattered across a handful of companies and universities. So if you're a mid-sized company and you want to prove something about your access control policies or your cryptographic code, you'd have to find and hire someone like that, and that's very hard.

The second is that the tools themselves have been pretty unforgiving. You'd write a specification in some formal language, and the theorem prover would come back and say "I couldn't prove it," and figuring out why, whether it's a bug in your code, a bug in your spec, or the tool needing a hint, that took a lot of skill and a lot of time. So the cost of getting to a proof was high.

The third, and this is the one people underappreciate, is the specification problem. Before you can prove anything, you have to agree on what "correct" means. And in most organizations, nobody actually knows precisely. The requirements live in people's heads, in design docs that contradict each other, in tribal knowledge. Formalizing that is as much a social process as a technical one.

What we found at AWS is that if you can hide the formal reasoning behind something the customer already cares about, like "can anyone on the internet reach this S3 bucket?", then you don't need them to be logicians. Tools like Zelkova and IAM Access Analyzer do billions of these checks, and customers never write a line of temporal logic.

And what's really exciting now is generative AI. LLMs are quite good at helping translate natural language into formal specifications, and at producing proof hints, and the provers in turn can check the LLMs' work so you're not just trusting a hallucination. That combination, I think, is what finally makes automated reasoning approachable for everybody, not just the companies that can afford a team of formal methods PhDs.

r001.rationale: The response describes specification ambiguity and the social effort of defining correctness, but it does not identify repeated clarification of domain experts’ beliefs as the main source of expense.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it comes down to a few things. Historically, formal reasoning tools have been incredibly powerful but also incredibly hard to use. You needed people with PhDs in logic or theorem proving, and those people are rare and expensive. If you were a large bank or a chip company or an aerospace firm, you could afford to hire a team of them, and the cost of a bug was high enough that it was worth it. For everyone else, the math just didn't work out.

The second piece is that the tools themselves were built by researchers, for researchers. The user experience was an afterthought. You'd have to learn a specialized language, encode your problem by hand, and then interpret some fairly cryptic output when the solver came back. There was a huge gap between "here's my policy" or "here's my program" and "here's the logical formula the tool understands." Bridging that gap was itself a skilled job.

And then there's the perception problem. For a long time formal methods got a reputation for being academic, for being slow, for not scaling. A lot of that was deserved in the eighties and nineties. But the underlying technology, SAT and SMT solvers in particular, made enormous leaps in the last twenty years. The tools got dramatically faster, but the perception lagged behind. So people assumed it was still out of reach when in many cases it wasn't anymore.

What's changing now, and what I find exciting, is that we can hide the logic behind interfaces people already understand. At AWS, for example, we built reasoning into things like IAM policy analysis and network reachability checking. Customers click a button and get an answer backed by a proof, and they never see a formula. That's the shift: moving from "learn to be a logician" to "just ask the question you already have." Once you do that, the economics change completely, and suddenly it's not just the largest enterprises who benefit.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the expense to scarce specialists, difficult tools, and manual encoding. It does not identify repeatedly clarifying what domain experts believe should be true as the main source of expense.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the expertise required. Traditionally, you couldn’t just pick up a tool and ask, “Is my system doing what I intended?” You needed someone who understood the mathematics, who could model the system, express the right properties, and then help the tool get through the proof. That’s a fairly rare combination of skills, and it’s expensive.

And there’s an investment in tooling. The thing you want to reason about is usually a real piece of software, with all sorts of details that don’t fit neatly into a mathematical model. Connecting those two worlds takes work. A large enterprise can spread that cost across a lot of systems, or justify it because a failure would be very costly. A smaller organization has a harder time making that investment.

So the challenge is to package the reasoning so that someone can benefit from it without having to become a formal methods expert. They should be able to ask a question in terms they understand and get an answer—or a concrete example of what could go wrong—that helps them do their job.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the expense to scarce expertise, tooling investment, and connecting software to mathematical models. It does not identify repeatedly clarifying what domain experts believe should be true as the main source of expense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the expertise required. Traditionally, you needed someone who understood both the system you were building and the mathematics behind the verification tools. Those people are rare, and getting the tools to work on a real system could require a substantial investment. A large enterprise could justify having a dedicated team; a smaller organization usually couldn’t.

There’s also the question of how you present the problem. Most developers don’t want to become experts in logic. They want to know, “Can this change break something? Can somebody access data they shouldn’t?” If we can put the reasoning behind an interface that lets them ask those questions in terms they already understand, then we can make it useful to a much wider audience.

r001.rationale: The response attributes expense to scarce expertise and the investment required to use verification tools. It does not identify repeatedly clarifying what domain experts believe should be true as the main source of expense.
